newsitem.title: COMOROS: Anjouan secessionists backed by fellow islanders.
newsitem.headline: Anjouan secessionists backed by fellow islanders.

text.p: Comoran security forces on Wednesday dispersed demonstrators on the Indian Ocean island of Moheli who were protesting in support of secessionists on the island of Anjouan, witnesses said.
They said supporters of separation of Moheli from the Islamic Republic of the Comoros took to the streets of the Moheli capital Fomboni, building barricades and burning tyres.

They raised the French flag on government buildings including the law courts before being dispersed by security forces. Moheli is the smallest of the three islands in the Comoro archipelago and has a population of some 25,000.
The Comoro Islands, with 190,000 people, became independent from France in 1975.

But many residents of Anjouan, Comoros' second island, and of Moheli say independence has brought only poverty, civil strife and coups, and want to return to French rule or break away from the Islamic republic.
In a statement, a committee campaigning for the autonomy of Moheli said it supported the struggle of the people of Anjouan for self-determination and condemned violence by security forces.
The commmittee called on the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) to organise a referendum on self-determination for Moheli and demanded the withdrawal of security forces from Anjouan.
Secessionists on Anjouan said on Tuesday they had elected their 75-year-old leader Foundi Abdallah Ibrahim as "president" of their breakaway state and feared troops on the island would intervene.
They told a news conference in the Anjouan capital of Mutsamudu that Fatima Abdere Mahe was appointed deputy president and Charikane Ahmed was put in charge of coordination with the president.
Former Comoran prime minister Mohamed Abdou Madi, 41, was appointed foreign minister for the new state of Anjouan.

Ibrahim, who has worked as both a Koranic teacher and a jeweller, was arrested by authorities for five days last month. He and three other secessionist leaders were freed after troops fired on demonstrators.
Anjouan's poverty contrasts with the relative prosperity of the island of Mayotte, which voted to remain French in 1975.
France has denounced the secessionists, saying the Anjouan situation is serious and could destabilise the whole region.
Comoran President Mohamed Taki said last Friday the islands would be given more autonomy and would be divided into communes.
Youths in the Anjouan capital Mutsamudu built barricades after the speech amid rumours of imminent military intervention to seize government buildings and arrest secessionist leaders.
The OAU appealed on Monday for calm on Anjouan and said it would send a special envoy to the Comoro Islands who would be mandated to talk to both the government and the secessionists.

Three people including a gendarme were killed on July 14 as demonstrators pressing for Anjouan to return to French rule or be independent clashed with security forces. Several were killed in March clashes.
